title: In 1947, a 'UFO incident' occurred in the middle of the New Mexico desert: decades later, the U.S. admitted the truth about Roswell
excerpt: The Roswell incident began in 1947 after the discovery of wreckage in New Mexico, and decades later the U.S. linked it to a secret military project.
content:
In 1947, some strange debris found in the New Mexico desert gave rise to one of the biggest mysteries in UFO history. The discovery was made near Roswell, a town that over the years would become synonymous with theories about extraterrestrial life and alleged US government cover-ups. However, behind the famous incident was a secret military program that could not be made public at the time.

It all began with Project Mogul, a US program developed during the early years of the Cold War. It used balloons equipped with microphones and other instruments to study the atmosphere and, in particular, detect possible sound waves from Soviet nuclear explosions. Washington feared the Soviet Union might develop its own atomic bomb, which it eventually did in 1949.

On June 14, 1947, rancher W. W. Brazel and his son discovered debris they could not identify in an area around 80 miles northwest of Roswell. Weeks later, the material came to the attention of local authorities, and the Roswell Daily Record reported that the nearby military base had recovered a “flying saucer.” The US Army quickly responded that the wreckage probably came from a weather balloon.

What really happened in Roswell?

For decades afterward, the story largely faded from public attention until the 1980 publication of The Roswell Incident brought the case back into the spotlight. Its authors argued that the balloon explanation had been a cover story, helping turn Roswell into one of the most famous cases in UFO culture.

The official explanation did not arrive until 1994, when the US Air Force published a report on the incident. According to the document, the debris was connected to NYU Flight 4, one of the balloon flights associated with Project Mogul, which had been launched on June 4, 1947, before crashing in the area. What had fueled theories about an extraterrestrial spacecraft for decades was ultimately explained as an accident involving a secret military program.

Despite the authorities’ explanation, Roswell never lost its association with extraterrestrials. The town continues to market itself as the “Alien Capital of the World,” has a museum dedicated to UFOs and has turned the story into its biggest tourist attraction. Retired Col. Albert C. Trakowski, who worked on Project Mogul, summed it up perfectly in one sentence: “People believe what they want to believe.”
